title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array
corePattern: Modified Binary Search on Rotated Sorted Array
interviewTips: Ask if array has distinct values and is guaranteed rotated from ascending sorted order with no duplicates, and confirm to return index or -1.
Trade-off: linear scan is O(n) simple but fails constraints; two-pass pivot-find plus binary search is clear but does two logs, one-pass halves constants and is preferred.
Edge-case tip: explicitly test n=1, no rotation, rotation at last index, target at lo-mid-hi boundaries, and target missing.

approaches.name: Approach 1: Brute Force Linear Scan
approaches.intuition: If we ignore rotation, the problem is just find target index. Scanning left to right always works and establishes correctness baseline.
approaches.theory: Iterate over all n elements and return first i with nums[i] == target, else -1. No assumption about order is used, so rotation is irrelevant. This is exhaustive search.

timeComplexity.explanation: Visit each element once in worst case where target missing or at end.

spaceComplexity.explanation: Only index variables, no extra storage.

edgeCases: Single element match returns 0, mismatch returns -1
Target missing returns -1 after full scan

approaches.name: Approach 2: Find Pivot Then Binary Search
approaches.intuition: Rotation creates two sorted halves split at minimum element. If we find the pivot, we know which sorted half can contain target and can run normal binary search there.
approaches.theory: Minimum element is the only place where nums[i] < nums[i-1] with wrap-around. Use binary search on property nums[mid] > nums[hi] to move lo to mid+1, else hi to mid, converging to pivot in O(log n). Then choose interval [pivot,n-1] if target between nums[pivot] and nums[n-1], else [0,pivot-1], and binary search that sorted interval.

timeComplexity.explanation: Pivot finding is O(log n) plus one binary search O(log n), total 2*log n.

spaceComplexity.explanation: Only lo, hi, mid, pivot pointers.

steps: Find pivot: lo=0 hi=6 mid=3 val7>2 => lo=4; lo=4 hi=6 mid=5 val1<=2 => hi=5; lo=4 hi=5 mid=4 val0<=1 => hi=4 => pivot=4
Binary search [4,6]: mid=5 val1>0 => hi=4; mid=4 val0==0 return 4

edgeCases: No rotation pivot=0 searches whole array
Pivot at n-1 means only last element is smallest
Target equals pivot value or nums[0] or nums[n-1] boundary

approaches.name: Approach 3: One-Pass Modified Binary Search
approaches.intuition: At any mid, at least one side of [lo,hi] is sorted because rotation can break only one side. Check which side is sorted and whether target lies inside it to discard half.
approaches.theory: If nums[lo] <= nums[mid], left half is sorted. If target in [nums[lo], nums[mid]) go left else go right. Otherwise right half must be sorted, so if target in (nums[mid], nums[hi]] go right else go left. Each step halves search space, preserving invariant that target if present is in [lo,hi]. Uses distinctness to decide sorted side unambiguously.

timeComplexity.explanation: Single binary search loop halves interval each iteration.

steps: lo=0 hi=6 mid=3 val7 !=0, left sorted 4<=7 but target 0 not in [4,7) => lo=4
lo=4 hi=6 mid=5 val1 !=0, left sorted 0<=1 but target 0 not in [0,1) => lo=6? Wait check: nums[lo]=0 <=1 and 0<=0<1 true so hi=4

edgeCases: Sorted no-rotation array behaves like normal binary search
Target at ends: nums[0] or nums[n-1]
Missing target between values returns -1 without infinite loop
